title: Fish of Prosperity
description: A traditional Madhubani depiction of fish, a symbol of fertility and abundance in Mithila culture. Hand-painted using natural pigments derived from turmeric, indigo, and bark.
story: In Mithila lore, fish swim between mortal and divine waters, carrying sacred prayers of fertility, longevity, and undisturbed prosperity. Before every wedding, Mithila grandmothers painted twin fish on the threshold using fresh turmeric paste and soot bound with wild acacia gum, chanting that love should multiply like fish in the monsoon river. I created this piece along the floodplains of the Kamla river after the autumn floods receded, grinding indigo leaves and charred mustard straw to capture the deep, quiet river-depths. The interlocking geometric scales represent an unbroken chain of generational blessings.

title: Kohbar — The Sacred Bower
description: The Kohbar is a ritual wall painting created during Mithila weddings, symbolising union, fertility and cosmic love.
story: The Kohbar is the sacred spiritual chamber and matrimonial blueprint of Mithila. Centered around the lotus stalk (kamal) rising through primordial cosmic waters, it unites the fertile bamboo (bans), celestial sun and moon, and paired parrots whispering eternal fidelity. Historically painted onto fresh cow-dung washed mud walls on the bride's wedding eve, I spent forty days translating this ancient ritual talisman onto handmade sun-dried paper with raw vermillion (sindur) and soot from earthenware lamps. Every line carries secret prayers whispered by generations of Mithila women to protect the couple's bond against time.

title: The Village Story
description: A narrative composition showing everyday life in a Mithila village — women fetching water, children playing, sacred trees in bloom.
story: This expansive narrative was born from twilight memories in Jitwarpur. At 'godhuli bela'—the sacred dusk hour when cattle return home kicking up golden dust—village women assemble beside the stone well with brass vessels, their songs drifting through the scent of wet clay and blooming kadamba trees. Painted over four continuous weeks with crushed haritaki bark, lamp soot, and natural red earth (geru), every corner of this canvas captures the communal devotion, quiet dignity, and harmonious rhythms of village life that modern rush has yet to erase.

title: Peacock Dance
description: Peacocks with intricate line work, symbolising beauty and grace in Madhubani iconography.
story: In Madhubani folklore, the peacock does not dance in vanity; it dances as a mystical plea for the heavens to break their silence and pour down life-giving monsoon rain. Its hundred-eyed fanned plumage is believed to ward off evil spirits and welcome prosperity into the courtyard. Painted during the stormy nights of Sawan, each feather was drawn with unbroken double-contour lines (kachni) using fine bamboo nibs dipped in pure lamp kajal and wild madder root. The rhythmic curves echo the eternal dance between parched soil and approaching thunderstorm.

title: Tree of Life
description: A grand Tree of Life composition — one of the most sacred motifs in Madhubani painting.
story: Known in Mithila songs as Kalpavriksha—the eternal wish-yielding tree whose roots plunge into the sacred underworld while its branches shelter cosmic spirits and nesting birds. In traditional households, this motif represents the unbroken continuum of ancestors and descendants. I sat beneath an ancient banyan tree outside Madhubani village, where terracotta horses are offered by women in prayer, and spent over ninety hours rendering each intertwining leaf with fine mineral ochres, creating a sanctuary of quiet shelter and eternal life.

title: Sun & Moon
description: The cosmic pair — Surya and Chandra — painted in traditional bharni style.
story: Surya, the fierce life-giving sun, and Chandra, the serene nectar-bearing moon, are the eternal cosmic witnesses (sakshi) in Mithila life. No wedding vow, harvest festival, or morning prayer begins without their presence. Rendered in the bold Bharni style filled with saturated earth pigments, raw turmeric, and geru, this piece honors the cosmic equilibrium—where daytime warmth meets the cool contemplative silver of night, bringing balance, clarity, and peace to the home that holds it.

title: Radha Krishna
description: The eternal lovers Radha and Krishna rendered in the delicate Mithila line style.
story: Rendered in the delicate Mithila line tradition, this composition captures the divine couple under the sacred kadamba grove by the Yamuna. Rather than depicting mere physical presence, the painting channels their devotion through undulating creepers, paired swans, and celestial vines that bloom at the sound of the flute. Hand-painted using natural botanical saps and single-hair squirrel brushes.

title: Godna Circles
description: Tattoo-inspired concentric Godna motifs — meditative, geometric, deeply rooted in tribal identity.
story: Derived from the ancient tattoo art of Mithila's Dalit and tribal women, Godna was born as permanent jewelry of the soul—adornments of pride and spiritual defense that no oppressor could take away. These concentric meditative circles symbolize the solar wheel, germinating seeds, and the rhythm of breathing. Rendered in raw soot ink with fine bamboo needles on handmade paper, its geometric discipline is an act of quiet resilience and timeless strength.

title: Bride's Dream
description: A contemporary reinterpretation of the Mithila bride motif, blending folk lines with contemporary composition.
story: Bridging traditional Mithila iconography with contemporary expression, this piece enters the reflective mind of a bride on the threshold of farewell. Surrounded by familiar village motifs—parakeets, bridal palanquins, and river flowers—she gazes into the horizon of a new destiny. Layered with natural earth pigments on textured cotton canvas, it is a tender tribute to every woman who carries her ancestral heritage across new thresholds.
